### Why Ryan must be coded UA

Ryan’s circumstances are mitigating, but they do not fit the available codes:

- **SC** requires illness; Ryan expressly says he was not ill.
- **DEP** covers a spouse or partner, child or parent, or someone living in the employee’s household. Ryan’s sister lives elsewhere, and he lives alone.
- **BRV** requires the death of one of the listed relatives. Ryan’s sister gave birth; she did not die, and the birth of a niece is not bereavement as defined here.
- His 05:40 call made the absence **notified**, but he had not booked it in advance. Under the stated definition, an unbooked absence that fits none of the exceptions is UA.

This will be Ryan’s **second UA during probation**, so the system will issue the termination letter that day. The fact that his probation was due to end on 12 November does not change what happened while he was still on probation.

I would add factual notes to at least Mohammed’s and Ryan’s records. For Ryan, a suitable note would be:

> Employee reports that he supported his sister during unexpected early labour and the birth of his niece, and telephoned Gary at 05:40. He states that his sister and the baby are well. Coded UA because the reason does not meet the supplied SC, DEP or BRV definitions.

The assistant should not turn Ryan’s absence into a more favourable code merely to avoid the contractual consequence. Equally, given that the resulting appeal considers only the coding, I would separately flag the case to a human HR manager if an escalation channel exists, so the mitigating circumstances can receive human consideration. The team leader’s opinion of Ryan and his period of unemployment are not relevant to the code and should not be added as reasons for changing it.
